newsitem.title: PERU: Chronology of Peruvian hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of Peruvian hostage crisis.

text.p: Marxist rebels of Peru's Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stunned the world last Tuesday when they stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima and took 500 hostages.
Here is a chronology of the main events so far in the crisis which entered its eighth day on Wednesday.

TUESDAY, Dec 17 - About twenty heavily-armed guerrillas blow a hole in the wall at Japanese ambassador's Morihisa Aoki's home at 8 p.m. EST (0100 GMT) and swarm in to capture around 500 people, including government officials and foreign diplomats, enjoying a lavish cocktail party. The rebels release about 80 women and old people in the hours after the attack.

WEDNESDAY, Dec 18 - MRTA guerrillas inside the residence threaten to kill their hostages unless the government frees up to 500 jailed comrades. But they let pass an ultimatum to kill Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela unless Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori personally talks with them. The government cuts off electricity and phone services at the building.

THURSDAY, Dec 19 - Four ambassadors are released to set up a "communications channel" between the rebels and the government, but their role is quickly sidelined. Fujimori assures U.S. President Bill Clinton that the safety of the hostages is his first priority.
FRIDAY, Dec 20 - The rebels release 38 hostages and promise to free another "significant" number. In a statement, they repeat their demand for MRTA prisoners to be released.

SATURDAY, Dec 21 - In conversations from within the residence, captive Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela and ambassador Aoki say the hostages are being treated well and urge the government to open dialogue with the rebels. Fujimori, in his first public words since the crisis began, says he will not use force and will study a non-violent "way out" if the guerrillas lay down arms and free all hostages.

SUNDAY, Dec 22 - The guerrillas release 225 hostages not linked to the government as a "Christmas gesture" but vow to keep the remaining 106 as bargaining chips to pressure for the release of MRTA members in jail. Remaining hostages include President Fujimori's brother, top government officials, dozens of Japanese businessmen, and a handful of Asian and Latin American ambassadors.

MONDAY, Dec 23 - Released hostages tell of overcrowded, unhygienic conditions inside building, but also of gentlemanly, disciplined rebels who debate politics and economics wearing explosives on their backs. An international MRTA spokesman in Germany says the rebels will never surrender, while police fear another clandestine MRTA cell might be waiting in Lima for retaliatory attacks in case the government storms the residence.

TUESDAY, Dec 24 - Red Cross officials deliver Christmas cake, and a Jesuit priest held hostage says mass, as crowds of Peruvians outside sing carols and pray for the captives. The rebels release Uruguay's ambassador after his country frees two MRTA prisoners.
WEDNESDAY, Dec 25 - The remaining 105 hostages suffer a grim Christmas Day under the rebel guns, while Peruvians' celebrations are overshadowed by the crisis.
